 Heat’s Adam Simon may have done it again with recent draft choice
 17 Comments 
 / By 
 Matt Hanifan 
 / November 17, 2026 
 (Mandatory Credit: Joe Murphy/NBAE via Getty Images) 
 When he was drafted, I was bullish on Miami Heat rookie Ryan Conwell.
 Ranked as the No. 37 player on my big board heading into the cycle, the tools and fit with Conwell were quite clear. He was one of the most gifted shooters in the class, shooting 38.4 percent from deep on 7.9 attempts per game over his final three seasons. He assumed an on-ball role for most of the season at Louisville, so his efficiency went down. But he was still competing defensively with improved ballhandling.
 All that said, my own expectations weren’t that Conwell was going to be one of Erik Spoelstra’s most trusted players three weeks into the season, which has been the case. And that trust isn’t born out of thin air, either. 
 Ryan Conwell has been one of the Miami Heat’s most impactful role players: 
 From Duncan Robinson to Max Strus to Pelle Larsson, the Heat have had a knack of finding and developing undiscovered gems into capable role players.
 Ryan Conwell may be the latest.
 Through 12 games, Conwell’s numbers may not scream impact.
 The 6-foot-4 guard is averaging 6.8 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.4 assists per game, shooting 35.8 percent from the floor and 32.7 percent from 3-point range. But his last six games have been remarkably encouraging, not only in the numbers, but in his impact, too.
 It’s difficult to quantify foot speed, feel and pure motor on defense. Conwell’s showcased all of those things; teams are putting the rookie to the test in space, and he’s done more than hold his own. He’s committed 2.5 fouls per game over that six-game span, but plenty of them come from the ubiquitous rookie whistle (tax).
 He’s not overly aggressive to the point where he’s consistently compromising his own (and team’s) defensive structure. Conwell’s still learning the angles of cutting off drivers, and he’s learning how to effectively limit the amount of space between him and the ballhandler.
 There’s still plenty of room to grow as an off-ball defender, but that’s always a steep adjustment, especially in Erik Spoelstra’s scheme. But if you’re going to play as a young player under the longtime head coach, you must defend.
 And Conwell’s done a good job adapting from the start of Summer League to now. Sure, there may be a few hiccups here and there. But the results are quite encouraging.
 Beyond that, it’s clear that Conwell is one of the Heat’s top shooters. The percentages aren’t very encouraging, but it sometimes takes rookies a little longer to adjust to the speed and conditioning that’s required at the level. Whenever he gets his feet under him, he’s an ignitable spot-up shooter capable of attacking closeouts and providing some secondary creation.
 The on-ball reps have been a mixed bag, but that’s normal. He was thrust into a primary creator role at Louisville because of Mikel Brown’s health, but that was not his forte. Conwell doesn’t have poor vision, but he doesn’t have a very tight or creative handle. Over time, hopefully that improves.
